title: Problem 1.1
statement_text: What is the minimum integer $f(k)$ such that every $f(k)$-chromatic oriented graph has an acyclic $k$-chromatic subgraph?
context_text: An oriented graph is an orientation of a simple graph (no 2-cycles), a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph, its chromatic number is that of the underlying undirected graph, and a subgraph is acyclic if it has no directed cycle. Burr conjectured that every $(2k-2)$-chromatic oriented graph contains a copy of every oriented tree on $k$ vertices (for tournaments this is Sumner's conjecture, resolved for large $k$ by Kühn, Mycroft and Osthus); Burr proved that chromatic number $(k-1)^2$ suffices, improved to $k^2/2-k/2+1$ by Addario-Berry, Havet, Sales, Reed and Thomassé. They observed that a $k$-chromatic oriented graph with no directed cycle contains every oriented tree of order $k$, and suggested that finding acyclic subgraphs of high chromatic number could yield improved bounds towards Burr's conjecture. Partitioning the edges into forward and backward edges of a vertex ordering gives two acyclic subgraphs, so $\chi(G_1\cup G_2)\le\chi(G_1)\chi(G_2)$ yields $f(k)\le k^2$, refined to $f(k)\le k^2-2k+2$, but substantially improving this seems to require new ideas. The authors show that the tournament version $g(k)$ (the minimum $g$ such that every $g$-vertex tournament has an acyclic $k$-chromatic subgraph) satisfies $k^{4/3-o(1)}\le g(k)\le k^{9/5+o(1)}$; since $f(k)\ge g(k)$, this approach cannot give bounds better than $k^{4/3-o(1)}$ for Burr's conjecture.
paper_title: Acyclic subgraphs of tournaments with high chromatic number

title: Problem 1.2 (Nassar–Yuster)
statement_text: What is the minimum integer $g\mathopen{}\mathclose{{}\left(k}\right)$ such that every $g\mathopen{}\mathclose{{}\left(k}\right)$-vertex tournament has an acyclic $k$-chromatic subgraph?
context_text: Nassar and Yuster introduced this tournament-restricted version of Problem 1.1, proved $k^{8/7}/4\leq g(k)\leq k^{2}-(2-1/\sqrt{2})k+2$, and further conjectured that $g(k)=o(k^{2})$. The paper under review resolves this conjecture in strong form.
paper_contribution: Proves $k^{4/3-o(1)}\leq g(k)\leq k^{9/5+o(1)}$, establishing $g(k)=o(k^{2})$ in strong form and simultaneously improving both the upper and lower bounds of Nassar and Yuster.
notes: The specific conjecture $g(k)=o(k^{2})$ appears in prose in the context immediately following Problem 1.2 and is the central target stated in the abstract.
paper_title: Acyclic subgraphs of tournaments with high chromatic number

title: Conjecture 4.1
statement_text: Every $n$-vertex tournament has an acyclic subgraph with chromatic number at least $n^{3/4-o(1)}$. That is, $g(k)\le k^{4/3+o(1)}$.
context_text: An oriented graph is an orientation of a simple graph (no 2-cycles), a tournament is an orientation of a complete graph, its chromatic number is that of the underlying undirected graph, and a subgraph is acyclic if it has no directed cycle. $g(k)$ is the minimum integer such that every $g(k)$-vertex tournament has an acyclic subgraph of chromatic number $k$ (a question of Nassar and Yuster, who proved $k^{8/7}/4\le g(k)\le k^2-(2-1/\sqrt2)k+2$ and conjectured $g(k)=o(k^2)$). The authors prove that every $n$-vertex tournament has an acyclic subgraph with chromatic number at least $n^{5/9-o(1)}$, i.e. $g(k)\le k^{9/5+o(1)}$, and construct (via a random orientation defined from a projective plane, following Rödl and Winkler) an $n$-vertex tournament in which every acyclic subgraph has chromatic number $O(n^{3/4}\log n)$, i.e. $g(k)=\Omega((k/\log k)^{4/3})$. They suspect the lower bound is closer to the truth. They also wonder whether the following simpler tournament attains the same bound: for $n=q^2$, on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ orient $ij$ ($i<j$) from $i$ to $j$ unless $q$ divides $i-j$, in which case from $j$ to $i$ (used by Nassar and Yuster for their lower bound).
paper_title: Acyclic subgraphs of tournaments with high chromatic number
